props.title: Pulse

sections.content: Pulse stands as an overlooked gem in the "technology gone wrong" subgenre, predating similar domestic horror films like Smart House (1999) and Demon Seed (1977). Director Paul Golding crafts a uniquely unsettling take on household electronics turning malevolent, focusing on a mysterious electrical force that infiltrates a suburban home. Unlike later films that dealt with AI like 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) or internet horror like Unfriended (2014), Pulse taps into a more primal fear of electricity itself - the invisible force we've invited into our homes.

sections.content: The film's strength lies in transforming mundane household appliances into sources of creeping dread. Where Poltergeist (1982) used the TV as a supernatural portal, Pulse treats the entire electrical grid as a malevolent entity. The film's practical effects hold up remarkably well, creating genuine tension from flickering lights, surging appliances, and deadly electrical accidents. Director Golding's approach influenced later technophobic horror films like Ghost in the Machine (1993) and Shocker (1989).

What sets Pulse apart is its focus on a child protagonist dealing with both supernatural threats and family dynamics. Like The Gate (1987) and Lady in White (1988), it balances genuine scares with coming-of-age elements. The film's suburban setting and emphasis on domestic technology predates similar themes in films like Small Soldiers (1998) and Toys (1992), where household items become threatening. sections.content: Pulse's influence can be seen in modern films dealing with technological anxiety. While movies like Transcendence (2014) and Upgrade (2018) focus on AI and human enhancement, Pulse's more grounded approach to technological horror resonates with films like Dark Water (2002) and One Missed Call (2003), where everyday technology becomes a conduit for terror. The film's premise of household infrastructure turning hostile influenced everything from Lights Out (2016) to Smart House (1999).
